\section{Linear regression}

Regression is a supervised machine learning method by which we can determine the existence and strength of the relationship between two or more variables. In particular, linear regression is a useful tool for predicting an quantitative response. Broadly, there are often two separate goals in regression:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item Prediction: fitting a model to observed data to predict outcomes for new observations;
  \item Inference: fitting a model to estimate and interpret the relationships between variables.
\end{itemize}

A clear scientific question should define our explanatory variable of interest ($x$), which is referred to as a predictor or independent variable. Our outcome of interest is referred to as the dependent variable or outcome ($y$). In linear regression, the dependent variable is always continuous; it cannot be a categorical variable. The explanatory variables can be either continuous or categorical.

Here are some examples of real-world regression problems:

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
  \item Predict tomorrow's stock market price given current market conditions and other possible side information;
  \item Predict the temperature at any location inside a building using weather data, time, door sensors, etc.;
  \item Predict systolic blood pressure based on the number of cups of coffee consumed per day;
  \item Predict the fuel efficiency of a car given engine parameters, speed, and road conditions;
  \item Predict daily electricity consumption in a household based on appliance usage, weather, and time of day;
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Simple linear regression}

Simple linear regression, or univariate linear regression, is a very straightforward approach for predicting a quantitative response $Y$ on the basis of a single predictor variable $X$.
